co_lower_wall.blurb: The Lower Wall is the biggest of the four sections at Hurd Creek Crag, a quiet single-pitch cliff in the Fraser Valley of Grand County at roughly 9,000 feet. Nineteen routes here are mostly bolted sport lines, with a pair of trad lines mixed in. Grades start around 5.6 and run up to 5.12, but the bulk sit between 5.7 and 5.11, so beginners through solid intermediates all find something. The gneiss is well regarded, and the lines are short, roughly 30 to 60 feet. A half-mile walk brings you to a fork in the trail, where you bear left for this wall. The cliff gets plenty of afternoon warmth.

co_playground_the.blurb: The Playground sits in Castlewood Canyon State Park on the East Rim, out on the plains southeast of Denver, grouped with neighbouring sectors near North Canyon Point. It is a mixed bag: about eleven sport routes, six trad lines, a top-rope and a lone boulder problem. Most of the climbing is in the low-to-mid 5.10s through 5.11, with a few 5.12 pitches and a couple of easy beginner-friendly options near the bottom of the scale. The walls are short and steep, on the conglomerate typical of this canyon, and some older bolts in the park are thin, so it pays to back up a single bolt.

co_mill_creek_wall.blurb: Mill Creek Wall is a compact alpine sport crag above Telluride, at about 10,800 feet, tucked at the head of the Mill Creek trail on the slope over the footbridge. Nineteen routes, mostly bolted with a few trad lines, stay under about 30 meters, so one rope and a rack of quickdraws is enough. The grades lean hard: nothing is easier than 5.9, and the best lines are in the 5.11 to 5.12 range. Expect a short, pleasant walk in, scree at the base of many starts, and rock that can be loose. Bugs are worth planning for in summer.

co_sheep_rock_summit_dome.blurb: The Summit Dome is the crown of Sheeprock, a granite dome complex in Colorado's South Platte country near Goose Creek and Molly Gulch, at roughly 8,800 feet. About twenty routes mix slab and face climbing, split between sport and trad, from a couple of easy fifth-class lines through 5.7 and 5.8 up to a handful of 5.10s. The standard summit route is an approachable two-pitch crack. Bolted slabs and blank, crystal-studded faces reward good friction. Reaching the base takes real effort: expect a long, steep hike with some scrambling. Bighorn sheep often bed down on top, where the potholes hold water.

co_stash_the.blurb: The Stash is a small bouldering sector within Hartman Rocks, the granite recreation area a few miles outside Gunnison. Nineteen problems are listed here, and the range is broad: a few easy warm-ups at the bottom, a solid middle in the V3 to V5 band, and a short tail of harder problems reaching V7. That makes it useful for mixed groups where one person wants easy laps and another wants something to project. Hartman as a whole offers sound granite in most places, though some patches are crumbly, so test holds before trusting them.

co_upper_y_traverse.blurb: Upper Y Traverse is a bouldering wall on Flagstaff Mountain above Boulder, at around 6,500 feet. It holds nineteen problems, with the grades centered on V1 to V4, a couple of harder ones near V7, a lone V10 and one easy problem for newcomers. The wall leans enough to stay climbable in drizzle. Besides the namesake traverse, expect a few highballs and some eliminate lines good for training. Walk down the hill to the east from the roadside pull-out and the wall is right in front of you.

co_tarot_wall.blurb: Tarot Wall is the leftmost section of the Second Tier in the Avalon zone of Boulder Canyon, at about 7,300 feet. Nineteen single-pitch routes run roughly 45 to 100 feet, mostly bolted sport lines with a few that blend gear and bolts. Nothing here is easy: the core is 5.10 and 5.11, with a stack of 5.12s and a couple of 5.13s above. The face has steep walls, roofs, aretes, cracks and corners. The Second Tier as a whole draws busy weekend crowds, and the base of many climbs is eroded with loose rock, so watch your belayer.
